item.title: Colombia’s president arrives at scene of supermarket hostage siege in tourist city
item.description:
Abelardo de la Espriella to take control of an operation involving scores of security personnel trying to free at least 20 hostages

Colombia’s president has arrived at the scene of an hours-long standoff between security services and gunmen holding at least 20 people hostage inside a supermarket in Cartagena, a popular tourist city.

Abelardo de la Espriella’s motorcade arrived in Cartagena on Tuesday night, Agence France-Presse reported, where he will ostensibly take control of a operation involving scores of officers, the navy and special forces.

item.title: Argentina enters technical recession after two quarters of contraction, the first since 2024
item.description: Argentina's economy has entered a technical recession, with two consecutive quarters of contraction, for the first time since the first half of 2024. GDP fell 0.6% in the second quarter, and INDEC's monthly activity indicator points to a contraction of about 1.8% between July and September.

item.title: The flag at waist height: the rules for visiting the Argentine Military Cemetery in the Falklands
item.description: Tourism authorities in the Falklands have asked operators to remind visitors of the rules of conduct at the Argentine Military Cemetery at Darwin, while a programme to repair its stonework, which has deteriorated over time, is being drawn up. The rules, set out in a bilingual document, allow the Argentine flag to be placed on graves but consider holding it above waist height a political gesture.

item.title: The Bukele method: will Salvadoran leader's strong-arm tactics work for Haiti?
item.description: Haitians are hailing the Bukele method. Citizens of the Americas’ poorest nation cheering the Salvadoran president’s ’shoot first, ask questions later’ method of dealing with the gangs that have overrun their country the past six years. Can the police force deployed actually restore law and order? We’ll ask about the latest in a decades-long list of efforts by the international community to support Haiti.

item.title: Car bomb destroys buildings in central Colombian city
item.description: A car bomb detonated in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio on Monday, destroying a local governor's office and surrounding buildings, President Abelardo de la Espriella said. The right-wing leader has conducted a major crackdown on the country's drug trade, in response to left-wing FARC rebels who have stepped up attacks over the past two years. item.title: José Adolfo Macías Villamar, alias ‘Fito’
item.description:
José Adolfo Macías Villamar, alias ‘Fito’

José Adolfo Macías Villamar, alias “Fito,” was the head of the Choneros, one of Ecuador’s most prominent criminal groups. He joined the Choneros during its rapid rise from a regional gang into one of the most powerful criminal organizations in Ecuador. His 2024 prison escape triggered a nationwide manhunt and a criminal and political crisis in Ecuador.

item.title: ‘Once installed, there’s no getting rid of it’: what Falklands oil plans mean for its seals, whales and penguins
item.description:
While Argentina and the UK dispute sovereignty over the islands and its vast oil reserves, environmentalists fear for one of the Atlantic’s richest ecosystems

From the air, the main Falkland Islands form two large, jagged shapes against the South Atlantic. East Falkland and West Falkland are surrounded by 778 smaller islands and islets east of Patagonia’s southern tip.

The archipelago, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, is home to large colonies of albatrosses and penguins. Its waters, with those of the Patagonian shelf, provide feeding grounds for sea lions, southern elephant seals and southern right whales.

item.title: Bank of England directors illegally profited from post-abolition enslavement in Cuba
item.description:
New research finds that the British-led Cobre Mining Company helped industrialise Manchester via copper deposits and enslaved African people

• Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds

British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research.

Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian Chris Evans has found.
